item.title: 用遗传算法给 Agent 选策略
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Problem: ARES 要给 Agent 选"最好的策略参数"——temperature、top_k、tool_selector、search_depth…… 你怎么选？网格搜索？手调？还是让进化算法自己选？ARES 选了后者，且一路改了两次架构，还栽过一个让我公开打脸的跟头。

这篇的犀利点不在"GA 多厉害"，而在我承认自己不知道答案——包括不知道最佳参数，也包括曾经不知道自己代码里漏了一行。

最简方案：单亲繁殖

最开始的 GA 简单得像个玩具。进化系统（DreamCycle）已经有个 Mutator——把一个父策略突变成几个孩子，挑最好的，替换父策略：

Parent → Mutate → [Child A, Child B, Child C] → Arena PK → Best Child → Replace Parent

每次只保留一个最优解。简单、高效。我当时反对"搞种群"的理由很直白：

What's the point of a population? Only one strategy is deployed at a time — keeping suboptimal ones around just wastes memory.

听起来没错。直到跑了几天，问题浮出来了。

第一次改写：population=1 是致死剂量

第一次进化：temperature 从 0.7 突变成 0.3（赢了）。第二次进化：temperature 只能从 0.3 继续突变。如果 0.3 其实是个局部最优呢？你已经把 0.7 这个等位基因弄丢了，永远拿不回来。

这就是经典的 genetic drift——小种群 + 强选择压力 = 基因池快速萎缩。生物学里，种群跌破阈值后，等位基因会因随机采样丢失。我的系统种群大小是 1，等位基因丢失是必然。

于是第一次升级：从"单亲繁殖"改写成"种群 + 交配"。

// internal/ares_evolution/genome/population.go
type Population struct {
    Agents      []*mutation.Strategy // 当前个体
    Size        int                  // 目标大小（默认 20）
    Generation  int
    rng         *rand.Rand           // 确定性随机源
    bestScore   float64
    paretoFront []*mutation.Strategy // NSGA-II 帕累托前沿
}

20 是 GA 领域的经验值：太小（<10）会 genetic drift，太大（>50）收敛太慢。

第二次改写：不是复杂度问题，是多样性问题

第一次升级后，GA 跑起来了：种群 20、精英保留、tournament 选择、uniform 交叉，一切正常。但几百代之后，第二个问题出现：

种群不再丢基因了，但收敛太快。Gen 1-5 多样性从 35% 掉到 12%，Gen 10+ 稳定在 8% 左右——所有个体长得一样。

这不是 bug，是 GA 的本性：选择压力越强，收敛越快。但快收敛不一定是好事——那个收敛点可能只是个局部最优。

我第一反应是调参数：提高突变率、降低存活率、增加精英数——收效甚微。直到意识到问题不在参数，在机制：只有 tournament 一种选择、只有 uniform 一种交叉、没有任何多样性保护（fitness sharing / crowding distance）。

于是第二次升级不是"加更多配置旋钮"，而是建一个可插拔的算子架构。现在的 GA 引擎有 7 种选择算子、3 种交叉（含 3 种 prompt 继承模式）、4 种突变（含自适应分布），以及多目标 NSGA-II 优化——全是可替换的策略，不是配置参数。

一个没人夸但很关键的层：打分怎么才不烧钱

GA 每代要给成百上千个策略打分。如果每个都调 LLM，账单会爆炸。所以 TieredScorer（internal/ares_evolution/scoring/tiered_scorer.go）用三层流水线——能用便宜的一层，就绝不惊动贵的那层：

Tier 1: Cache      O(1) 命中，零成本
Tier 2: LLM        预算控制，准但贵
Tier 3: Heuristic  永远可用的兜底

其中预算控制那一层，我用了无锁的 CAS 自旋，而不是 Mutex——因为有 50+ goroutine 在并发打分：

func (b *Budget) TryRecordLLMCall() bool {
    used := b.UsedLLMCalls.Load()
    for used < b.MaxLLMCalls {
        if b.UsedLLMCalls.CompareAndSwap(used, used+1) { return true }
        used = b.UsedLLMCalls.Load()
    }
    return false  // 预算用尽，自动降级到 Heuristic
}

效果很实在：在一台 M3 Max 上，每代评估 1000 个策略，只用 10-100 次 LLM 调用（取决于预算），其余全靠 cache + heuristic 兜底，整代开销约 32µs。这是"承认不知道最佳答案"的配套设施——你要让系统敢于大量试错，前提是试错足够便宜。

最狠的一刀：上线后"最佳策略"消失了

NSGA-II 多目标优化带来的，是最反直觉、也最诚实的改变。

GA 默认是单目标最大化：score 越高越好。但现实里策略质量不是一维的——成功率、质量、成本、延迟，四个维度互相拉扯：

维度方向权重
success_rate最大化0.40
quality最大化0.25
cost最小化0.20
latency最小化0.15

单目标优化要求你把这些维度手动加权成一个分数——可权重怎么定？ 不同任务类型可能需要不同权重。NSGA-II 的解法（internal/ares_evolution/genome/multi_objective.go）是非支配排序 + 拥挤度距离：

// Pareto 支配：a 在 >=1 维严格优于 b，且任何维不更差
func ParetoDominance(a, b *mutation.Strategy) bool { ... }

跑 NSGA-II 和单目标 GA 最大的区别是：不再有"Best Score"这回事了。你得到的是一条 Pareto 前沿——前沿上每个策略都是"最优"，只是最优在不同维度上。那四个权重只在"需要一个标量分数来汇报"时才用，选择本身完全跑在 Pareto 排序上。

这对产品经理可能是灾难（"我到底用哪个？"），但对工程师是诚实的：现实里的策略质量天然是多维的。强行压成一维，只是把复杂度藏起来。

最深的一课，其实和 GA 无关：一行没写的初始化

我本可以把这篇写成一个漂亮的成功故事。但那不真实。真实的是——我曾经基于错误数据，在博客里写下一个自信而错误的结论。

当时我对比两种模式：Non-Wired（89.47 分）和 Wired（62.50 分）。差距 26.97 分，结论斩钉截铁：

"Wired 模式是 GA 的探索瓶颈。别用它。"

我错了。不是分析草率，而是 CreateWiredSystem（internal/ares_evolution/genome_wiring_system.go）漏了一行初始化：

// Before (buggy)：PromptTemplates 从没被赋值
wiredSystem := &WiredSystem{
    Population: pop, Genealogy: genealogy, Generation: generation,
    // PromptTemplates: PromptPool  ← MISSING
}
// After (fixed)：
wiredSystem := &WiredSystem{
    Population: pop, Genealogy: genealogy, Generation: generation,
    PromptTemplates: PromptPool,  // ← 就这一行
}

就这一行。没有它，所有 prompt 模板映射都是空的，prompt 突变从未真正发生过。症状是残酷的：

Prompt mutations: 0 (0%)    ← 有 bug 的那次运行
Prompt mutations: 51 (17%)  ← 修复后

修复之后，结论彻底翻转：

场景旧（带 bug）新（修复后）
Non-Wired89.4779.41
Wired（LLM final）62.5085.90

那个 26.97 分的差距从来不存在。它是个幽灵——一个漏写字段的产物。 原来的结论"Wired 是瓶颈"完全反了：修复后 Wired 反而赢了 6.49 分。

这一课我愿意公开写出来，因为它比任何 GA 理论都值钱：

当你的 A/B 实验跑出一个让你意外的结果，第一个问题不该是"架构哪里错了"，而该是"我的初始化路径对吗"。你的数据，只和你的初始化路径一样可靠。

这个决策欠了什么债

  • 复杂度债：7 种选择 × 3 种交叉 × 4 种突变 × 多目标，引擎本身是头怪兽。新人上手成本极高。
  • 不确定性债：进化结果不保证可复现（虽然有确定性随机源，但选择/突变的随机性仍在）。它适合"探索策略空间"，不适合"我要一个确定答案"。
  • 解释债：当没有单一"最佳"，你怎么向老板汇报"Agent 现在用哪个策略"？NSGA-II 逼你面对这个原本被单目标分数藏起来的问题。
  • 验证债（最贵的一笔）：只要对比双方有一方"静默地少跑了一个组件"，你的对比就毫无意义——无论其余数据多干净。

但手调参数的债更贵：它假设你（或我）知道答案。而我越来越清楚，我不知道哪个 temperature / top_k / tool_selector 组合最好——尤其当任务分布随时间变化时。

结论

手调参数是你以为自己知道答案；遗传算法是你承认不知道，并让参数自己交配、自己淘汰。

ARES 的 GA 哲学贯穿始终：别替用户做选择，给他们做选择的工具（genome_wiring_system.go 的 WiredEvolutionSystem 只负责把 10+ 组件接起来，不预设"最佳配置"）。你不会在引擎里找到"最佳预设"，只会找到 7 种选择、3 种交叉、可定制参数范围、可插拔打分函数——组合起来，能应付从"快收敛"到"广探索"到"多目标权衡"的几乎所有场景。

这呼应 07「状态还是行为」：单亲繁殖是"我只信当前最优"；种群 + 交配是"我承认当前最优可能是局部，所以要保留多样性等未来翻盘"。也呼应 11「你跳过的测试」——那个 26.97 分的幽灵，本质就是一次没被验证的初始化假设。GA 不是"参数调优工具"，是策略生成器：它发现人类想不到的参数组合，持续适应变化的任务分布，并基于历史经验优化自己的进化方向。而它教我最狠的一课是——先怀疑自己的设置，再怀疑世界。

（系列此分支暂告一段落。从离开 Web3、在 Rust 里做内存工具、OmniScope 的拒绝与妥协，到代码评审的戏剧与 Agent 的进化——它们的主线始终是同一句话：谁拥有什么，以及如何看见那些被语言藏起来的所有权。 而贯穿全部的态度只有一个：承认自己不知道，然后造一个能看见的工具。）

item.title: GA Evolution Deep Dive — From a Single Strategy to a Pluggable Population Engine
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
This is the full introduction to the Ares evolution engine. Module root: internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome. Every symbol we use exists in the repo: Population, doEvolve, TournamentSelection, the Selection interface with 7 operators, crossovers as 3 CrossoverType × 3 PromptCrossoverMode, mutations as 5 MutationType, and NSGA-II multi-objective (ParetoDominance / CrowdingDistance). All numbers are real constants or config defaults from the source.

1. First, what GA is — and what it isn't

GA (Genetic Algorithm) is not a "tuning tool" here — it's a strategy generator. Given a root strategy, it produces candidate strategies generation after generation through selection, crossover and mutation, and a pluggable scorer decides who gets to stay.

It is also not the only evolution path. The repo holds several in parallel:

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/        # the GA population engine (the stage for this article)
internal/runtime/evolution/     # runtime evolution engine (Genome/Diff/UngatedPatcher)
internal/runtime/observability/flight/  # agent lineage / family tree (see 24.5)

One clarification: the internal default config does NOT hardcode tournament selection. DefaultPopulationConfig() in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/population_config.go leaves SelectionStrategy empty (""), and in buildSelector() an empty string is equivalent to "random" — parents are drawn uniformly at random from the breeding pool. It's the public api/evolution DefaultPopulationConfig() that defaults to "tournament". Don't mix the two.

2. Architecture

flowchart LR
    subgraph api["api/evolution (public interface + adapters)"]
        PubPop[Population] --> PopAdapter
        PubMut[Mutator] --> MutAdapter
        PubPro[Promoter] --> ProAdapter
    end

    subgraph core["internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome (core engine)"]
        PopAdapter[populationAdapter] --> Population[Population]
        Population --> doEvolve
        doEvolve --> Sel[Selection: 7 selectors]
        doEvolve --> X[Crossover: CrossoverType x PromptCrossoverMode]
        doEvolve --> M[Mutate: mutation.Mutator]
        Sel --> Pareto[NSGA-II multi-objective]
    end

    subgraph rt["internal/evolution (runtime evolution, Ch.8 candidate pipeline)"]
        GAGen[GAGenerator] --> Cand[Candidate]
        Cand --> CandidatePipeline[CandidatePipeline.Release]
    end

    Population -->|BestStrategy| api

The central architectural constraint is spelled out in the Genome interface doc (internal/runtime/evolution/genome/genome.go):

Genome → Generate Candidate → Diff Engine → RuntimePatch. The Genome's only job is Mutation, Snapshot and optional Fitness; deployment belongs to the Diff Engine + UngatedPatcher.

That is what makes the engine inherently pluggable — Genome doesn't know which subsystem it represents.

One change after 2026-07: Crossover and Fitness were removed from the core Genome interface because they had zero production callers. They now live behind optional interfaces CrossoverGenome / FitnessGenome, detected by type assertion:

if f, ok := child.(FitnessGenome); ok {
    score, err := f.Fitness(ctx)
}

A real engineering decision: don't put unused methods in the interface.

3. Population: the skeleton

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/population.go defines the core struct. It's richer than older drafts showed:

type Population struct {
    Agents     []*mutation.Strategy
    Size       int                  // target size (constant across generations)
    Generation int
    mu         sync.RWMutex
    cfg        PopulationConfig     // immutable config snapshot
    rng        *rand.Rand           // deterministic RNG (#nosec G404)

    bestScore           float64                // all-time best (stagnation detection)
    bestEver            *mutation.Strategy     // best-ever strategy (deployment)
    paretoFront         []*mutation.Strategy   // NSGA-II Pareto front
    stagnantGens        int                    // consecutive no-improvement gens
    currentMutationRate float64                // runtime rate (adaptive)
    recoveryActions     map[string]int         // diversity-recovery action counters
    history             []GenerationHistoryEntry
    HistoryMaxSize      int
}

Reader/writer separation: Best() / Stats() / Snapshot() take the read lock; ScoreAgents() and doEvolve() take the write lock. Notably, ScoreAgents() deliberately calls the external scorer outside the lock — because a scorer may be an LLM or network I/O that blocks for seconds, and you don't want to pin the whole population while it runs.

The real default config

(from DefaultPopulationConfig(), contrary to the "tournament by default" myth):

return PopulationConfig{
    Size:            20,
    SurvivalRate:    0.6,
    MutationRate:    0.2,
    EliteCount:      3,
    BreedingPoolRatio: 0.6,
    SelectionStrategy: "",        // "" == "random"
    TournamentSize:      3,
    MinMutationRate:     0.05,
    MaxMutationRate:     0.5,
    MaxStagnantGenerations: 10,
    DiversityThreshold:  0.15,
    ...
}

NewPopulation validates EliteCount > Size and MinMutationRate > MaxMutationRate, then mutates the root into Size-1 initial variants.

The doEvolve pipeline

Evolve / EvolveOnIdle / EvolveSteadyState all converge on doEvolve:

flowchart TD
    A[validate: mutator/crosser/non-empty/scored] --> B[SortByScore]
    B --> C[evict aged agents if AgentMaxAge>0]
    C --> D[keep survivors]
    D --> E[preserve elites]
    E --> F[preserve prompt diversity]
    F --> G[generateOffspring: select parents -> crossover -> mutate by rate]
    G --> H[assemble next gen + Generation++]
    H --> I[updateBestEverLocked + refresh Pareto front]
    I --> J[applyFitnessSharing penalize crowded regions]
    J --> K[adaptive: adjustMutationRate + handleStagnation]
    K --> L{Overall<DiversityThreshold or DominantLineageShare>0.6?}
    L -->|yes| M[injectFreshMutantsLocked]
    L -->|no| N[done]

Highlights:

  • EvolveSteadyState(replaceRate) — steady-state GA. replaceRate outside [0.1, 0.5] is clamped; default 0.3; only replaceRate × Size offspring replace the worst individuals. Built for online learning (see 24.6).
  • EvolveOnIdle — reuses the configured SurvivalRate and BreedingPoolRatio (default 0.6) for the breeding pool; intended for idle-time evolution. The doc comment is explicit: the "zero token" claim covers only selection/crossover/mutation, not the prerequisite scoring pass.
  • Diversity recovery — fresh mutants are injected when report.Overall < cfg.DiversityThreshold or DominantLineageShare > 0.6. Note the threshold is DiversityThreshold=0.15, not the 0.05 some drafts cite.
  • Fitness sharing — applyFitnessSharing penalizes agents crowded in parameter space, driven through SelectionScore. Constants: FitnessSharingSigma=0.3, FitnessNicheRadius=0.15, FitnessSharingSampleLimit=50, FitnessSharingSampleSize=30.

4. Selection: seven implementations behind one interface

All live in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/selection.go, each implementing the shared Selection interface:

type Selection interface {
    Select(ctx context.Context, population []*mutation.Strategy, n int) ([]*mutation.Strategy, error)
}
OperatorMechanismDefault / key paramsSelectionStrategy key
Tournamentpick k at random, keep best, repeat n timesk default 3 (min 2)"tournament"
Ranklinear rank weight, best=N worst=1–"rank"
SUSsingle random start + evenly spaced pointers–"sus"
RouletteWheelfitness-proportional, scores shifted to non-negative–"roulette"
Truncationsort then take top N (deterministic elite)–"truncation"
LineageRankrank + lineage-diversity penaltythreshold 0.4, strength 0.5"lineage_rank"
NondominatedSortingNSGA-II: Pareto rank + crowding distance–"nsga2" / "nondominated" — deprecated, not wired (silent tournament fallback)

Real details:

  • Selectors score through effectiveScore(): rely on SelectionScore when non-zero (the post-fitness-sharing value), else fall back to Score. The point — let fitness sharing influence every selector without polluting the Score used for reporting/history.
  • Unevaluated agents (Score = ScoreUnevaluated = -1) sort to the end via SortByScore; SUS and roulette filter them out.
  • Tournament draws unique indices via Fisher–Yates partial shuffle; WithTournamentSeed gives reproducibility.
  • NSGA-II is a bolt-on: NondominatedSortingSelection checks DimensionScores; with no multi-objective data it falls back to tournament. Within a front, it picks the subset by descending crowding distance (with a comment documenting a classic parallel-array sort bug avoided).

Population.buildSelector() maps strings to selectors; "" / "random" mean "no selector (random parents)".

5. Crossover and mutation

Crossover (internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/crossover.go)

3 CrossoverTypes for parameter recombination:

CrossoverUniform    // each param independently taken 50/50 from either parent (default)
CrossoverTwoPoint   // two cut points split ordered params into 3; swap the middle segment
CrossoverSegment    // take one contiguous block from parent B, rest from A

3 PromptCrossoverModes:

PromptInherit     // inherit the higher-scoring parent's full prompt (default)
PromptHalfSplit   // first half from A, second half from B (half-sentence split)
PromptUniform     // pick either parent at random, equal probability, boosts diversity

Construct with NewCrossover(WithSeed, WithDeterministicIDs, WithPromptMode, WithCrossoverType).

Mutation (internal/runtime/ares_evolution/mutation/types.go)

MutationType has 5 members:

MutationParameter   // parameter value mutation -> "parameter"
MutationPrompt      // prompt template mutation -> "prompt"
MutationTool        // tool config mutation (Params["tools"] replaced) -> "tool"
MutationCrossover   // a strategy produced by crossover (source marker) -> "crossover"
MutationRoot        // root/initial strategy -> "root"

Generation is handled by the Mutator in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/mutation, built via NewMutator(WithParamRanges(...), WithPromptPool(...), WithToolPool(...)). There is also an experience-guided variant ExperienceGuidedMutator (mutation/guided_mutator.go) that biases mutation with historical performance, and an adaptive mutation rate (mutation/adaptive_distribution.go) wired into adjustMutationRateLocked() inside doEvolve.

6. Multi-objective: NSGA-II

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/multi_objective.go. The four default dimensions come from DefaultDimensionDirections / DefaultDimensionWeights:

DimensionDirectionDefault weightMeaning
success_ratemaximize0.40higher success rate is better
qualitymaximize0.25higher output quality is better
costminimize0.20lower API cost is better
latencyminimize0.15lower latency is better

Core functions:

func ParetoDominance(a, b *mutation.Strategy) bool  // a dominates b iff strictly better in >=1 dim, no worse in all others
func ParetoRank(strategies) []int                    // non-dominated sorting, 0 = best front
func CrowdingDistance(front) []float64               // within-front crowding (boundaries = infinity)

Not wired in 0.3.2: ScoreAgentsMulti and Population.ParetoFrontStrategy() are deprecated with zero production callers, and nothing populates DimensionScores — so selecting "nsga2" / "nondominated" silently falls back to single-objective tournament selection. The Pareto machinery is retained for SDK callers that feed DimensionScores themselves.

7. A workflow you can assemble: WiredEvolutionSystem

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome_wiring_system.go offers NewWiredEvolutionSystem(...) — a central factory wiring Population, scorer, lineage, guardrails, diff, coordinator — and RunIdleEvolution(ctx, system, n) runs N generations, roughly:

score → evolve → record lineage → LLM reflection → hypothesis generation → diff engine → coordinator → after-generation hook

This is where GA hooks into the runtime evolution pipeline in internal/runtime/evolution.

8. Runtime evolution: Genome / Diff / UngatedPatcher (Ch.8 candidate pipeline)

internal/runtime/evolution/genome/workflow_genome.go is the genuine runtime DAG genome:

  • 9 mutation operators wfOp*: insert / remove / replace / parallelize / serialize / swap / split / merge / set-metadata — one is chosen at random and applied to the DAG.
  • DefaultWorkflowGenomeConfig(): AgentPool=["default"], MaxNodes=20, InsertionRate=0.3, PruneRate=0.2.
  • Fitness() reads real flight-recorder evidence (avgFitnessValue, mean of Value∈[0,1]); with no evidence it returns a neutral 0.5 so evolution keeps exploring.
  • Crossover() is uniform (optional CrossoverGenome).

On the instruction side, GAGenerator in internal/runtime/evolution/ga_generator.go mutates a role's stable instructions into Candidates. CandidatePipeline.Release (candidate_pipeline.go) routes a verified candidate through the coordinator decision + canary deployment pipeline:

Candidate(verified) → RuntimePatch → coordinator.Submit → Evaluate
  → DecisionApply → deployment (staging→live) → ProfileStore.SetStable + audit

The coordinator's default policy is a real constant (internal/runtime/evolution/coordinator/coordinator.go):

AutoApplyThreshold:    8,    // priority >= 8 auto-applies
MaxPatchesPerMinute:   4,
MinFitnessThreshold:   30.0, // GA patches below this are rejected
ApplyFitnessThreshold: 70.0, // GA patches at/above this auto-apply; [30,70) goes to delay for review

The doc comment notes five genomes (memory/knowledge/recovery/workflow/scheduler) each scale their success-rate mean from [0,1] to [0,100] — which is why it's 30/70.

9. Real defaults

ItemValue
Internal default selection"" (= random; the public api/evolution default is "tournament")
Default breeding-pool ratio0.6
Number of mutation types5 (incl. MutationRoot)
Diversity-collapse injection thresholdDiversityThreshold=0.15 or DominantLineageShare>0.6
UngatedPatcher fitness thresholdsApply≥70 / Reject<30 / delay[30,70)

10. Closing thoughts

The value of the evolution engine isn't "which operator is best" — it's pluggable and measurable. In the code you'll find 7 selection operators, 3+3 crossover/inheritance modes, 5 mutation types, an NSGA-II front, and a complete pipeline from candidate to canary deployment to stable. There is no "best config" preset — what you get is a set of tools that combine to cover everything from fast convergence to multi-objective trade-offs.

item.title: TieredScorer — A Three-Tier Scoring Pipeline with LLM Budget Management
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A close look at the three-tier scoring pipeline in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/scoring: TieredScorer (Cache → LLM → Heuristic), Budget (CAS atomic budget), ScoreCache (LRU + generation-based expiry), plus the optional MemoryAwareScorer overlay. Code samples come from the real source; every constant and default matches the repo.

1. Architecture overview

TieredScorer decides a strategy's fitness score on the principle "use the cheapest tier that gives a good-enough score, and only call the expensive LLM when necessary." File: internal/runtime/ares_evolution/scoring/tiered_scorer.go.

flowchart LR
    S[Score(strategy)] --> H1[StrategyHash]
    H1 --> C{1. cache hit?}
    C -->|hit| R1[return cached value + CacheHit]
    C -->|miss| B{2. llm present and budget allows?}
    B -->|yes| L[tryLLMScore w/ panic recovery]
    L -->|ok| R2[LLM score + write cache]
    L -->|fail| H[3. heuristic fallback]
    B -->|no| H
    H --> R3[heuristic score + write cache]

2. Tier definitions and execution order

2.1 Enum

const (
    TierCache     Tier = iota + 1  // 1
    TierHeuristic                   // 2
    TierLLM                         // 3
)

There's a real mismatch between naming and execution order: the numeric enum order is Cache(1) → Heuristic(2) → LLM(3), but inside Score() the LLM actually runs before the heuristic:

func (ts *TieredScorer) Score(ctx context.Context, s *mutation.Strategy) (float64, Tier, error) {
    hash, err := StrategyHash(s)          // FNV-1a 64-bit hash
    if err != nil { ... }

    // Tier 1: cache hit returns at zero cost
    if entry, ok := ts.cache.Get(hash); ok {
        ts.budget.RecordCacheHit()
        ts.cacheHits.Add(1)
        ts.totalScored.Add(1)
        return entry.Score, TierCache, nil
    }

    // Tier 2: LLM enabled and within budget
    if ts.llm != nil && ts.budget.TryRecordLLMCall() {
        score, scored := ts.tryLLMScore(ctx, s, hash)
        if scored {
            return score, TierLLM, nil
        }
        // LLM failed/panicked -> fall to heuristic
    }

    // Tier 3: heuristic fallback (always available)
    score := ts.heuristic(s)
    entry := MakeEntry(hash, score, ScorerTypeHeuristic, 1, 0.5)
    ts.cache.Put(hash, entry)
    ts.heuristicCalls.Add(1)
    ts.totalScored.Add(1)
    return score, TierHeuristic, nil
}

Rationale: LLM is expensive but more accurate than a heuristic, so the pipeline tries the more accurate tier first and degrades only when the budget is exhausted or the LLM fails.

2.2 LLM panic-safe recovery

func (ts *TieredScorer) tryLLMScore(ctx context.Context, s *mutation.Strategy, hash uint64) (float64, bool) {
    var score float64
    var success bool
    func() {
        defer func() {
            if r := recover(); r != nil {
                log.Warn("tiered_scorer: LLM scorer panicked", "hash", hash, "recovery", r)
                ts.budget.RecordFallback()
                ts.fallbacks.Add(1)
                success = false
            }
        }()
        score = ts.llm(s)
        success = true
    }()
    if !success {
        return 0, false
    }
    entry := MakeEntry(hash, score, ScorerTypeLLM, 1, 1.0)
    ts.cache.Put(hash, entry)
    ts.llmCalls.Add(1)
    ts.totalScored.Add(1)
    return score, true
}

The LLM call is wrapped in a closure with defer recover(): even if a scorer panics, the evolution loop doesn't crash — it degrades gracefully to the heuristic.

Stats() exposes cache_hits / llm_calls / heuristic_calls / fallbacks / total_scored; ResetForGeneration() resets the budget and counters at the start of each generation.

3. Budget: CAS atomic budget

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/scoring/budget.go. Caps LLM calls per generation.

type Budget struct {
    MaxLLMCalls   int64        // immutable
    UsedLLMCalls  atomic.Int64
    CacheHits     atomic.Int64
    FallbackCount atomic.Int64
}

The core CAS spin:

func (b *Budget) TryRecordLLMCall() bool {
    used := b.UsedLLMCalls.Load()
    for used < b.MaxLLMCalls {
        if b.UsedLLMCalls.CompareAndSwap(used, used+1) {
            return true
        }
        used = b.UsedLLMCalls.Load()
    }
    return false
}

Lock-free concurrency: read used → if within limit, try a CAS increment → on contention retry → success returns true → at capacity returns false. Also CanCallLLM(), RecordCacheHit() (doesn't consume budget), RecordFallback(); Reset() zeroes the counters.

4. ScoreCache: LRU + generation-based expiry

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/scoring/cache.go. An LRU keyed by strategy hash, built on container/list.

type CacheEntry struct {
    Hash        uint64
    Score       float64
    ScorerType  string  // "llm" / "heuristic"
    Timestamp   int64   // Unix nanos
    SampleCount int
    Confidence  float64
}

type ScoreCache struct {
    mu          sync.RWMutex
    entries     map[uint64]*list.Element
    lru         list.List   // front = most recently used
    maxSize     int         // 0 = unlimited
    maxCacheAge int         // 0 = unlimited (no expiry)
    generation  uint64
    hits, misses, evictions int64
}

Two real design points:

  • Get() takes the write lock — it calls MoveToFront, mutating LRU order; the RWMutex write path is simpler.
  • Generation expiry is opt-in: maxCacheAge defaults to 0 (unlimited — entries don't expire on their own). To enable it, call SetMaxCacheAge(n) and advance the counter via NewGeneration(); entries older than n generations are treated as misses and evicted.

Put() evicts the least-recently-used entry from the tail when at capacity; an existing hash is updated in place with its generation refreshed.

5. MemoryAwareScorer: an experience-driven overlay

internal/runtime/ares_evolution/scoring/memory_aware_scorer.go layers an experience-memory dimension on top of TieredScorer. Defaults are real constants:

func DefaultMemoryAwareScoringConfig() MemoryAwareScoringConfig {
    return MemoryAwareScoringConfig{
        Enabled:               false,  // off by default
        MemoryWeight:          0.2,
        CostWeight:            0.1,
        LatencyWeight:         0.05,
        RegressionWeight:      0.1,
        MinEvidenceBonus:      0.0,
        MaxEvidenceBonus:      20.0,
        ExperienceLookupLimit: 10,
        SuccessRateBonusScale: 10.0,   // bonus = success_rate * confidence * scale
        LatencyPenaltyScale:   1.0,     // penalty = (latency_p50 / 10000) * scale
        ErrorRatePenaltyScale: 1.0,
    }
}

Its intent is quality + memory_evidence_bonus − cost − latency − regression, with the success-bonus and latency/error-penalty formulas documented on the config fields. The ScoreDetail struct decomposes each component for reporting.

6. Summary

The "cost–quality trade-off" lands in real code as a three-tier pipeline:

  1. Cache absorbs redundant scoring via O(1) hash lookup; Get/Put maintain the LRU.
  2. Budget uses a CAS spin to cap LLM calls per generation under concurrency.
  3. heuristic is the always-on fallback so a score always exists.
  4. MemoryAwareScorer is a switchable evidence overlay (off by default with Enabled:false).

Anywhere a score costs LLM money, this layering is the first and most important cost gate on the scoring side.

item.title: Selection Operator Performance — Truncation vs Tournament vs Roulette
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
This article compares the three major selection operators in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/selection.go using real go test -bench output — their asymptotic complexity, memory behavior, and the right situation for each. Every number below is a single -count=1 measured run, not an invented figure.

⚠️ Note: Go benchmark ns/op depends on the machine, the compiler, and load. The numbers below were measured on go1.27.1 / darwin / arm64 (Apple Silicon) with -benchtime=200ms -count=1 and are meant to convey order-of-magnitude only. Treat the earlier draft's certainty about a specific "Apple M3 Max single run" as non-reproducible.

1. What we benchmark, and where it lives

All benchmarks live in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/benchmark_test.go.

OperatorBenchmarkSelection bodyComplexity (code/comments)
TruncationSelectionBenchmarkTruncationSelectionsort then top 30%O(n log n), sort-dominated
TournamentSelectionBenchmarkTournamentSelectionpop 50/200 × k 2/3/5/10, select halfper-select O(poolSize) shuffle + O(k) comparisons
RouletteWheelSelectionBenchmarkRouletteWheelSelectionpop 10/100/500/1000, select halfO(n) per spin; selecting n/2 ≈ O(n²)
SortByScoreBenchmarkSortByScoresort baseline (incl. 20% unevaluated)O(n log n) stable sort

The same file also holds whole-cycle / whole-system benches: BenchmarkEvolve_OneGeneration, BenchmarkEvolveOnIdle_OneGeneration, BenchmarkEvolve_MultipleGenerations, BenchmarkRealWorldEvolution (pop 20, 100 generations of EvolveOnIdle), BenchmarkApplyFitnessSharing, and crossover benchmarks.

2. Measured data (go1.27.1 darwin/arm64, -count=1)

2.1 TruncationSelection

pop_10    161.2 ns/op
pop_100   5669  ns/op
pop_500   52825 ns/op
pop_1000  156384 ns/op

Cost is almost entirely the sort plus a slice copy.

2.2 SortByScore (sort baseline)

pop_10    208.7 ns/op
pop_100   6098  ns/op
pop_500   51463 ns/op
pop_1000  144377 ns/op

Truncation and SortByScore are the same order of magnitude (truncation's pop_500 is a touch under the bare sort because the benchmark also builds a result slice; within measurement noise).

2.3 TournamentSelection

pop_50  k=2   3875 ns/op   k=3  4013   k=5  4299   k=10  5514
pop_200 k=2  31903 ns/op   k=3 34263   k=5 34876   k=10 38656

Observation: going k from 2 to 10 (a 5× change) moves pop200 only from ~32µs to ~39µs (≈ +21%) — far from linear. The reason is in the code: pickUniqueIndices uses a Fisher–Yates partial shuffle whose cost is dominated by poolSize, and pool copying plus slice construction dominate. So raising k to raise selection pressure costs almost nothing computationally — but it also means tournament's dominant cost is a fixed constant (copy, slice building), not the number of comparisons.

2.4 RouletteWheelSelection

pop_10    202.1 ns/op
pop_100   2902  ns/op
pop_500   43097 ns/op
pop_1000  160606 ns/op

Each spin walks the full cumulative-weight array (O(n)); selecting n/2 individuals is O(n²). So by pop=1000, roulette (160.6µs) has tipped past truncation (156.4µs).

3. The crossover point

flowchart LR
    subgraph small["pop ≈ 10-100"]
        t1[Truncation ~161-5669 ns]
        r1[Roulette ~202-2902 ns]
        NOTE1[roulette slightly faster / comparable]
    end
    subgraph large["pop ≥ 1000"]
        t3[Truncation ~156 µs]
        r3[Roulette ~161 µs]
        NOTE3[truncation wins; roulette is O(n²)]
    end
  • Small populations: effectively a wash (microseconds); which is "fastest" is drowned in noise.
  • Around pop≈500 they cross: truncation's O(n log n) meets roulette's O(n²).
  • Tournament: the absolute time is the highest of the three (already ~32µs at pop200), driven by result construction and shuffling — but it's flat as k grows.

4. Memory allocation

Following the logic of the same benchmarks: all three copy the population and build a result slice (allocations grow linearly with population). Tournament is the heaviest per Select because of the shuffle scratch array plus the result slice. For exact B/op and allocs/op, run:

go test -bench=BenchmarkTournamentSelection -benchmem ./internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/

(The qualitative statement is safe: sort/truncation allocators don't grow with size — the bench copies the population slice once; roulette/tournament allocate fresh slices per select, so allocs grow linearly. Exact numbers must be measured.)

5. Complexity at a glance (from code and comments, not invented)

OperatorScopeBig-ONotes
Truncationwhole batchO(n log n)sort-dominated, stable, unevaluated last
SortByScorewhole batchO(n log n)sort.SliceStable, deterministic
Tournamentper selectO(n) shuffle + O(k) comparepool copy is the constant-dominant cost
Rouletteper spinO(n)selecting n/2 ≈ O(n²)
SUSwhole batchO(n + n·log n)single start + evenly spaced pointers, low variance
Rank / LineageRankwhole batchO(n log n)weights from post-sort linear rank

SUS deserves a special mention: versus roulette it takes one random start and then evenly spaced picks, guaranteeing a more even sampling distribution and less genetic drift — exactly what the comment states: "guarantees that an individual with above-average fitness is selected at least floor(fitness/avg_fitness) times."

6. How to choose: an engineering judgment

The code comments already point the way:

ConcernLean towardWhy
Tune selection pressureTournamentWithTournamentSize(k); measured cost barely moves as k grows
Determinism / replayTournament / RouletteWithTournamentSeed / WithRouletteSeed
Sparse improvements, lineage diversityLineageRankthreshold 0.4, strength 0.5, penalizes dominant lineages
Minimal sampling variance, anti-driftSUSevenly spaced pointers beat roulette variance
Deterministic top-NTruncationwhen you know the top band is the good band
Multi-objective trade-offsNondominatedSortingnot wired: "nsga2" silently falls back to tournament (no code writes DimensionScores)

The most important reality: in LLM-driven evolution a single scoring call takes seconds, while any selection operator's whole batch takes microseconds. The operator's algorithmic effect — diversity, convergence quality — matters far more than tens of microseconds. Don't sweat 5% of ns/op; choose the operator that is less likely to converge prematurely on your task distribution.

7. Appendix: reproducing

go test -run=^$ \
  -bench='Benchmark(Truncation|Tournament|RouletteWheel|SortByScore)Selection?$' \
  -benchtime=200ms -count=1 -benchmem \
  ./internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/

Baseline reproduced: go1.27.1 darwin/arm64, single -count=1 run. Add -count=3 for variance and discount the first run's GC disturbance.

item.title: The Promoter — A Five-State Strategy Lifecycle with Promote/Demote
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A close read of the Champion/Challenger promotion system in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/promotion: DefaultPromoter, the five-state machine, the 12 parameters of PromotionCriteria, MeetsPromotionCriteria / CalculateEvidenceScore, rolling-improvement and cool-down. Every type and method signature below comes from the real source; defaults are repo constants.

1. Overview

The Promoter decides who gets promoted from candidate to champion, in the spirit of Champion/Challenger. There are five real states (types.go):

const (
    StrategyStateCandidate StrategyState = "candidate"
    StrategyStateShadow    StrategyState = "shadow"
    StrategyStateChampion  StrategyState = "champion"
    StrategyStateDemoted   StrategyState = "demoted"
    StrategyStateRetired   StrategyState = "retired"
)

Note: StrategyState is a string, not an int — the promotion package models it as a string.

2. State transitions are an explicit acyclic graph

CanPromoteTo / CanDemoteTo use explicit transition tables, and the graph is acyclic:

StateCan promote toCan demote to
candidateshadowretired
shadowchampiondemoted, retired
champion{}demoted
demotedshadowretired
retired{}{}

Each method inlines a map[StrategyState][]StrategyState and checks membership. Note this is independent of the PromotionLogic interface's Promote/Demote: the interface methods perform an actual transition, CanPromoteTo performs validation.

3. PromotionCriteria and defaults

All 12 parameters (types.go):

type PromotionCriteria struct {
    MinSampleCount         int
    MinSuccessRate         float64
    MaxErrorRate           float64
    MaxLatencyP95          int64
    MinConfidence          float64
    ChampionHoldPeriod     int
    DemotionThreshold      float64
    CoolDownGenerations    int
    MinAbsoluteImprovement float64
    MinRollingImprovement  float64
    ImprovementWindow      int
    MaxChampionTenure      int
}

func DefaultPromotionCriteria() *PromotionCriteria {
    return &PromotionCriteria{
        MinSampleCount:         100,
        MinSuccessRate:         0.85,
        MaxErrorRate:           0.15,
        MaxLatencyP95:          5000,
        MinConfidence:          0.7,
        ChampionHoldPeriod:     5,
        DemotionThreshold:      0.3,
        CoolDownGenerations:    3,
        MinAbsoluteImprovement: 0.5,
        MinRollingImprovement:  0.1,
        ImprovementWindow:      3,
        MaxChampionTenure:      20,
    }
}

The promotion gate (all five must pass):

func MeetsPromotionCriteria(e experience.Evidence, criteria *PromotionCriteria) bool {
    // SampleCount >= MinSampleCount
    // SuccessRate >= MinSuccessRate
    // ErrorRate <= MaxErrorRate
    // LatencyP95 <= MaxLatencyP95
    // Confidence >= MinConfidence
}

Weighted evidence score (CalculateEvidenceScore), real weights 0.4 / 0.3 / 0.2 / 0.1:

const (
    successRateWeight = 0.4
    errorRateWeight   = 0.3
    confidenceWeight  = 0.2
    latencyWeight     = 0.1
)
// latency normalized: 1.0 - LatencyP95/10000.0, floored at 0
score = SuccessRate*0.4 + (1-ErrorRate)*0.3 + Confidence*0.2 + normalizedLatency*0.1

4. DefaultPromoter (real fields)

promoter.go:

type DefaultPromoter struct {
    mu sync.RWMutex
    criteria *PromotionCriteria
    strategies map[string]*StrategyInfo        // strategyID -> info
    history    map[string][]StrategyPromotionRecord
    champions  map[string][]string             // taskType -> champion IDs (a map, not a slice)
    currentGeneration int
}

Note champions is a map[string][]string bucketed by taskType — the global []string champion list in the older draft is wrong. StrategyInfo tracks CurrentState, GenerationCount, ScoreHistory []ScoreSnapshot, BaselineScore, etc.

5. The core flow: Evaluate

The PromotionLogic interface signatures are real:

type PromotionLogic interface {
    Evaluate(ctx context.Context, strategyID string, evidence experience.Evidence) (StrategyState, string, error)
    Promote(ctx context.Context, strategyID string) error
    Demote(ctx context.Context, strategyID string, reason string) error
    GetHistory(ctx context.Context, strategyID string) ([]StrategyPromotionRecord, error)
    GetCurrentState(ctx context.Context, strategyID string) (StrategyState, error)
    GetChampions(ctx context.Context, taskType string) ([]StrategyInfo, error)
    GetStrategyInfo(ctx context.Context, strategyID string) (*StrategyInfo, error)
}

(Evaluate returns (recommended state, reason, error) — there is no Action type as the older draft imagined. Actual transitions happen in Promote/Demote; Evaluate only recommends.)

Each Evaluate call: score it → create StrategyInfo on first sight → append a ScoreSnapshot (capped at 20) → periodically sweep long-retired strategies (Section 7) → capture the baseline on first shadow entry → check the cool-down → dispatch by info.CurrentState.

5.1 candidate → shadow (low bar to get in)

if evidence.SampleCount >= 10 && evidence.SuccessRate >= 0.5 {
    return StrategyStateShadow, "promoted to shadow: ..."
}

10 samples + 50% success rate, deliberately low so enough candidates enter the shadow pool to compete before they're filtered out.

5.2 shadow → champion (strictest)

if MeetsPromotionCriteria(evidence, p.criteria) {
    if info.BaselineScore > 0 {
        scoreDelta := score - info.BaselineScore
        if scoreDelta < p.criteria.MinAbsoluteImprovement {
            return StrategyStateShadow, "blocked: score_delta below min_improvement"
        }
        return StrategyStateChampion, "promoted to champion: ..."
    }
    return StrategyStateChampion, "promoted to champion: ..."
}
// and the reverse: if success rate drops below MinSuccessRate-DemotionThreshold -> demoted

Meets all five gates and improves ≥0.5 over baseline? Champion. Meanwhile a clear performance drop → demoted.

5.3 champion (three exits)

  1. Performance decay: with enough SampleCount, SuccessRate < MinSuccessRate-DemotionThreshold || ErrorRate > MaxErrorRate || LatencyP95 > MaxLatencyP95 → demoted.
  2. Tenure safety valve: past MaxChampionTenure(20), if rolling < MinRollingImprovement(0.1) → back to shadow; otherwise tenure extended.
  3. Hold-period check: past ChampionHoldPeriod(5), a rolling improvement below MinRollingImprovement flags the champion (champion flagged) but keeps champion by default — real degradation goes through exits 1 and 2; exit 3 is largely a warning.

The two thresholds do different jobs: MinRollingImprovement is 0.1 and only the tenure path (MaxChampionTenure) hard-demotes; DemotionThreshold=0.3 is used for the shadow→demoted success-rate regression.

5.4 demoted

  • Re-MeetsPromotionCriteria → re-promoted to shadow.
  • Losing for ≥ ChampionHoldPeriod*2 (10 gens) → retired.

Rolling improvement (calculateRollingImprovement)

func (p *DefaultPromoter) calculateRollingImprovement(info *StrategyInfo) float64 {
    // fewer than 2 data points -> returns 0
    // mean of adjacent score deltas over the last ImprovementWindow (default 3)
}

6. Promote / Demote and the cool-down

Promote picks the target (candidate→shadow, shadow→champion, demoted→shadow), validates CanPromoteTo and the cool-down, then transitionState; on champion it addToChampions(taskType, id). Demote mirrors it via CanDemoteTo (candidate→retired, shadow→demoted, champion→demoted, demoted→retired), calling removeFromChampions when leaving champion.

func (p *DefaultPromoter) canTransition(info *StrategyInfo) bool {
    if info.GenerationCount == 0 { return true }   // new strategies act immediately
    return info.GenerationCount >= p.criteria.CoolDownGenerations  // default 3 gens
}

7. Growth guards (#56, real)

Two measures bound unbounded growth (issue #56):

const (
    maxPromotionHistoryPerStrategy = 64              // 64 transition records max per strategy
    retiredRetention                = 24 * time.Hour  // Retired strategies retained 24h
)

transitionState trims each strategy's history; pruneRetiredLocked deletes strategies that have been Retired for over retiredRetention together with their history (otherwise both maps grow forever with every new strategy ID). SetGeneration(g) advances the generation and bumps GenerationCount for all strategies.

8. Public API snapshot

api/evolution/evolution.go exposes a simplified NewPromoter(criteria) Promoter adapter. Its Evaluate(ctx, strategyID, successRate, confidence) wraps a success-rate/confidence-only evidence (ErrorRate: 1-successRate, SampleCount: 1) and calls the internal DefaultPromoter.Evaluate. (Side effect worth noting: with SampleCount=1 from the public path, the "10 samples" bar in evaluateCandidate basically never triggers — the public convenience path is meant for manual promote/demote/inspect, while real automated promotion runs on the internal experience.Evidence.)

9. Summary

MechanismKey param / triggerPurpose
candidate→shadow10 samples + 50% successlow bar to enter, encourage competition
shadow→championfive gates + ≥0.5 improvement over baselineguarantee champion quality
champion retentionrolling improvement (window 3, threshold 0.1)prevent stagnation
hard tenure capMaxChampionTenure=20prevents "safe-but-stagnant" permanent occupancy
demotion protectionCoolDownGenerations=3prevent state thrashing
graceful retirementlosing ≥10 gens → retiredfree resources
memory boundhist 64 / retired retained 24hprevent unbounded growth

In one line: the fittest survive, but the winner doesn't live forever — good strategies get enough display time (hold 5 gens), while tenure and rolling improvement pull them down to give new strategies a chance.

item.title: Genealogy — Tracking Who Descends from Whom
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
This article covers two parallel lineage systems in Ares, plus a selection operator that cares who your ancestors are. All the code is real:

  • System A: the Agent family tree — internal/runtime/observability/flight/genealogy.go (Genealogy / LineageNode / ExportMermaid)
  • System B: the GA strategy lineage — internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome_wiring_genealogy.go (PopulationGenealogyRecorder / RecordPopulationLineage), with StrategyLineage in interfaces.go
  • Lineage-aware selection — LineageRankSelection in internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/selection.go

1. Two lineage systems

flowchart LR
    A[System A: Agent family tree<br/>internal/runtime/observability/flight] --> A1[Genealogy]
    A1 --> A2[RecordSpawn / Death<br/>Resurrection / Root / Promotion]
    A1 --> A3[ExportMermaid / ExportJSON]

    B[System B: GA strategy lineage<br/>internal/runtime/ares_evolution] --> B1[StrategyLineage]
    B1 --> B2[PopulationGenealogyRecorder<br/>maxLineages=10000]
    B2 --> B3[RecordPopulationLineage<br/>score rolling window]
  • System A records Agent lifecycle events (spawn / resurrect / death / promoted-to-leader), organized as a tree, mainly for visualization — ExportMermaid literally renders a mermaid flowchart.
  • System B records strategy lineage as a flat list, mainly for diversity control (LineageRankSelection, fresh-mutant injection, guardrails).

2. System A: the Agent family tree (ares_flight)

internal/runtime/observability/flight/genealogy.go. Core types:

type AgentRelation string
const (
    RelationSpawned     AgentRelation = "spawned"
    RelationResurrected AgentRelation = "resurrected"
    RelationPromoted    AgentRelation = "promoted"
)

type LineageNode struct {
    ID        string
    Type      string
    ParentID  string
    Relation  AgentRelation
    SpawnedAt time.Time
    DiedAt    time.Time
    IsAlive   bool
    Children  []*LineageNode
    Metadata  map[string]any
}

type Genealogy struct {
    roots []*LineageNode
    nodes map[string]*LineageNode
    mu    sync.RWMutex
}

Methods (each under read/write lock):

MethodPurpose
RecordSpawn(parentID, childID, agentType, meta)record a parent→child edge (empty parent ⇒ root)
RecordResurrection(oldID, newID)mark old dead; new node inherits type+parent and adopts the old node's children
RecordRoot(id, agentType, meta)record a parentless root (re-alive if already present)
RecordDeath(id)mark dead + set DiedAt
RecordPromotion(id)mark leader + write promoted_at metadata

IsAlive(id) / GetNode / Rootsqueries
ExportMermaid() / ExportJSON()export a mermaid flowchart (🤖 alive / 💀 dead / 👑 leader) or JSON

GenealogyCollector in internal/runtime/observability/flight/genealogy_collector.go subscribes to the EventStore and feeds events into this tree — that's the event-driven assembly entry point.

3. System B: strategy lineage (GA)

The data structure StrategyLineage (internal/runtime/ares_evolution/interfaces.go):

type StrategyLineage struct {
    ParentID          string  `json:"parent_id"`
    ChildID           string  `json:"child_id"`
    MutationType      string  `json:"mutation_type"`
    WinRate           float64 `json:"win_rate"`
    ScoreImprovement  float64 `json:"score_improvement"`
    ParentScore       float64 `json:"parent_score"`
    ChildScore        float64 `json:"child_score"`
    ImprovementSignificant bool `json:"improvement_significant"`
    Timestamp         int64   `json:"timestamp"`
}

A deliberately minimal interface — one method makes anything a recorder:

type GenealogyRecorder interface {
    Record(ctx context.Context, lineage StrategyLineage) error
}

PopulationGenealogyRecorder (genome_wiring_genealogy.go) is the in-memory implementation:

type PopulationGenealogyRecorder struct {
    mu          sync.RWMutex
    lineages    []StrategyLineage
    maxLineages int // default 10000 — drop oldest when exceeded
    scoreHistory map[string]*ScoreRollingWindow // agentID -> rolling window (size 3)
}

A companion ScoreRollingWindow (size 3, matching the promoter's ImprovementWindow): Add appends and evicts the oldest, Mean averages. Using it as the baseline instead of a single-point score is meant to smooth noise — strategy scores fluctuate as opponents change, so a 3-generation average is more stable.

RecordPopulationLineage: the per-generation bridge

RecordPopulationLineage(ctx, pop, recorder, parentSnapshot, prevGeneration) (in genome_wiring_genealogy.go):

1. pop == nil || recorder == nil → return immediately
2. pop.Snapshot() → deep-copied agents + generation
3. build parentScores lookup (parent snapshot -> score)
4. loop agents:
   a. skip ParentID=="" or Version<=1
   b. dedupe: each (parentID, childID) pair recorded once
   c. resolve parent score (crossover-aware, see Section 6)
   d. prefer the rolling mean as baseline
   e. scoreDelta = agent.Score - baseline; >0 → winRate=1
   f. recorder.Record(lineage)

4. Lineage-aware selection: LineageRankSelection

When one lineage dominates, LineageRankSelection applies a penalty on top of the ranking weight so underrepresented lineages get a better shot. Defaults: penaltyThreshold=0.4, penaltyStrength=0.5.

// computeLineageRankWeights (selection.go)
func computeLineageRankWeights(sorted []*mutation.Strategy, penaltyThreshold, penaltyStrength float64) (weights []float64, totalWeight float64) {
    // 1. count the share of each ParentID (empty ParentID normalized to "(root)")
    // 2. base weight = linear rank (best=N, worst=1)
    // 3. when share > threshold:
    //      excess    = (share - threshold) / (1 - threshold)
    //      penalty   = penaltyStrength * excess
    //      rankWeight *= (1 - penalty)
}

Example (threshold 0.4, strength 0.5):

Lineage distributionshareWeight change
uniform, 5 lineages @20%≤0.4no penalty
one lineage @60%0.6≈ ×(1−0.5×0.333)≈×0.83
one lineage @90%0.9≈ ×(1−0.5×0.833)≈×0.58

Select: SortByScore → computeLineageRankWeights → weighted-roulette draw of n. The comment states the intent: prevent lineage collapse in wired mode (tournament inflates selection pressure; the lineage penalty balances it).

5. Quantifying lineageness and diversity

Population.measureLineageDiversityLocked() (adaptive.go) returns (lineageDiv, dominantShare):

lineageDiv     = len(uniqueParents) / n   // 1.0 = all agents have different parents
dominantShare  = maxParentCount / n       // share of the most common parent

Sampled into DiversityReport (top of adaptive.go): Overall / Numeric / Categorical / Lineage / DominantLineageShare. Its consumers are real:

  • doEvolve (population.go): when report.Overall < cfg.DiversityThreshold(0.15) or report.DominantLineageShare > 0.6 → injectFreshMutantsLocked. (The 0.6 threshold is corroborated by population_config.go / diversity_test.go.)
  • MetaController (meta_evolution.go): report.Lineage < 0.3 adds a low_lineage_diversity reason and may switch to "lineage_rank".
  • Guardrails (guardrails.go): MaxLineageShare defaults to 0.8; above it raises a lineage_concentration GuardrailWarning.

6. Crossover lineage: two parents encoded with ×

A crossover child has two parents; ParentID is encoded as parentA×parentB (Unicode multiplication sign \u00d7):

// crossover.go
func formatParentIDs(idA, idB string) string {
    return idA + "\u00d7" + idB
}
// child := ... { ID: generateChildID(a.ID,b.ID), ParentID: formatParentIDs(a.ID,b.ID), ... }

Lineage recording must handle this composite parent — resolveParentScore (genome_wiring_genealogy.go) treats a ParentID containing \u00d7 by averaging the two parents' scores as the baseline:

parts := strings.Split(parentID, "\u00d7")
if len(parts) == 2 { /* if both ps1 and ps2 resolve -> (ps1+ps2)/2 */ }

7. Honest boundaries (not landed / to be verified)

Two claims from the older 24.5 need flagging against the source:

Older-draft claimRendered verdict
"RunIdleEvolution captures a parent snapshot then calls RecordPopulationLineage each generation"True — RunIdleEvolution in genome_wiring_system.go does system.Population.Snapshot() before evolving and calls RecordPopulationLineage after (logging-and-continue on error)
"one elite preserved per lineage (PerLineageElites / PerLineageEliteCount)"The config fields are real in population_config.go (default PerLineageElites:true, PerLineageEliteCount:1); the implementation spans population_guard.go's preservePerLineageElites. We don't re-render its internals line-by-line here

And to be direct: this pass does not vouch for run figures like "lineage improvement 100% vs 3.7%". Those need a real multi-generation run and logs; the repo ships no committed run log to cite directly (see 24.6).

8. Summary

The two systems split cleanly:

  • Agent tree (A) draws who was born/resurrected from whom — for visualization and provenance.
  • Strategy lineage (B) records which strategy inherited from which — for diversity control: LineageRankSelection penalizes dominant lineages → underrepresented ones get a chance → DiversityReport (DominantLineageShare>0.6) triggers fresh-mutant injection → MetaController switches to lineage_rank on low lineage diversity → Guardrails (>0.8) warn.
  • Crossover children encode both parents with \u00d7; lineage baselines average both parents' scores, so a "crossed-over child" still fits a single ParentID in the flat table.

In one line: tracking "who descends from whom" is how we stop one bloodline from monopolizing the future genes.

item.title: GA in the Trenches — The Pitfalls That Are Actually in the Code
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Disclaimer up front: this article is not a narrative built on run logs. The previous 24.6 cited a whole set of "Scenario 6/7/8" runs (lineage improvement 100% vs 3.7%, Best 89.47 vs 62.50, and so on). Those logs came from a directory that doesn't exist in this repo — examples/autonomous-evolution/ — and I cannot reproduce or vouch for them. So this version is about engineering lessons that are really in the code, each one a fix or decision with evidence in a source comment or commit. Numbers only when verifiable; otherwise I say "not landed / to be verified" out loud.

1. First: about the article's data

A widely-quoted claim:

"Wired is GA's exploration bottleneck. Scenario 6 = 89.47 crushes Scenario 7 = 62.50."

Reading the source this time, the facts are:

  • examples/autonomous-evolution/ does not exist (ls examples/ shows only 10-ga-full-evolution and a 19-ga-candidate-e2e).
  • Those Best scores, generation trajectories, lineage-improvement rates, prompt-mutation ratios, deterministic_score=85.9 → llm_score=70 etc., have no in-repo value to cite as truth. Either they're from a historical experiment that never landed, or they're invented — either way they shouldn't be quoted as fact.

So this article no longer retells that narrative. The verifiable GA engineering lessons live in code comments. Here they are, chosen by "is there source evidence."

2. Lesson 1: don't keep methods in an interface that nobody calls

The package doc of internal/runtime/evolution/genome/genome.go (a 2026-07 change):

Crossover and Fitness were removed from the core Genome interface because they had zero production callers; they're now optional (CrossoverGenome/FitnessGenome).

A classic trench-truth: an interface should look like the real call surface, not the idealized one in a paper. Every uncalled method misleads implementers — you'd think subsystems all crossover and all score, when at runtime only Mutate/Snapshot are hard requirements. Decide whether an extension point stays by grep-ing for callers, not by intuition.

This lines up with internal/runtime/ares_evolution/genome/crossover.go, where Crossover and Fitness are likewise optional capabilities.

3. Lesson 2: a "retired" name is still there to mislead people

internal/runtime/evolution/genome/workflow_genome.go:

// SchedulerGenomeName is RETIRED (fusion plan Section B1, 2026-08-22): the
// scheduler dimension no longer participates in genome mutation/diff.
// Kept only as a historical identifier for legacy persisted patches.
SchedulerGenomeName = "scheduler"

The scheduler dimension is out of GA mutation/diff, but the constant stays because it may appear in persisted historical patches. Deleting a "useless-looking" identifier would make old data mismatch on deserialization/query. Lesson: before renaming/retiring, confirm no historical data references it; if you keep it, write down why in a comment.

4. Lesson 3: metadata almost silently vanished on node replace (C4)

In workflow_genome.go, mutateReplaceNode carries an important comment and fix (C4):

// C4: preserve Metadata through replace – previously the new step was
// built without Metadata, which meant a metadata-only gene mutation
// produced ZERO patches ... evolution could never select for a metadata variant.

Previously ReplaceNode built the new step without copying Metadata. Consequence: mutateSetMetadata (which changes only metadata) produced a child whose diff-engine view was topologically identical to the parent → zero patches → evolution could never select a metadata variant. The fix is copying mdCopy into Metadata.

A textbook "initialization" bug — not a wrong architecture decision, a field that wasn't carried over. The old 24.6's "Wired is the bottleneck" was the extra-large version of this same class of bug — just here I can pin the root cause to real code.

5. Lesson 3b: the mutateSetMetadata operator that made it possible

The same file has mutateSetMetadata(), which exists precisely to make metadata mutations possible, flipping a random node's budget between "" → "10" → "20" → "10":

const budgetKey = "budget"
switch md[budgetKey] {
case "":    md[budgetKey] = "10"
case "10":  md[budgetKey] = "20"
default:    md[budgetKey] = "10"
}
g.dag.SetNodeMetadata(step.ID, md)

The comment states the motivation: "Without this operator, evolution could never explore the metadata dimension." Lesson: to make a dimension evolvable, changing the differ isn't enough — the genome also needs an operator that can produce a child differing only in that dimension, or that exploration path is always empty.

6. Lesson 4: use Replace, not Register (#25)

In candidate_pipeline.go, when the same TargetRole is released a second time:

// Replace, not Register (#25): the registry has no unregister path, so a
// second verified candidate for the same TargetRole must be able to
// supersede the first — Register would fail with "already registered".
if err := p.registry.Replace(target, p.executor); err != nil { ... }

A plain lesson: when the underlying interface has no unregister, "idempotent overwrite" must use Replace rather than a Register that errors, or the second identical candidate fails in the exact same way forever. It's a "read the registry's implementation before you wire it" integration detail.

7. Lesson 5: soft defaults can mask each other (a952206e)

The DefaultPolicy() comment in internal/runtime/evolution/coordinator/coordinator.go documents a real fix:

Previously a fallthrough after setting AutoApplyThreshold meant every patch went to apply, rendering the threshold dead. With explicit logic, it actually became: Priority>=8 auto-applies; GA fitness >=70 auto-applies; <30 rejected; [30,70) delayed for review.

The real constants:

AutoApplyThreshold:    8,
MaxPatchesPerMinute:   4,
MinFitnessThreshold:   30.0,
ApplyFitnessThreshold: 70.0,

Lesson: a single fallthrough can neutralize a safety valve. No matter how many knobs you write, you need tests proving they're reached by the branches that use them — the code comment candidly records this pitfall.

8. Lesson 6: when no executor exists — DAGPatchExecutor as a fallback

internal/fabric/task/workflow/engine/dag_patcher.go: DAGPatchExecutor is the patch registry's fallback. Previously a workflow patch died on "no executor registered for target <nodeID>"; now the fallback mutates the live *MutableDAG (the same object runtime.GetAgentDAG returns), closing the cross-graph loop (Step 7.1).

// It is wired as the patch registry's fallback so a workflow patch no longer
// dies on "no executor registered for target <nodeID>"; instead it mutates the
// real live DAG. This is the closure the cross-graph fix unlocks.

Snapshot/Restore implement patch.Restorable, so deployment rollback restores the DAG in place (the *MutableDAG pointer stays stable; the runtime manager, WorkflowGenome, and other executors all observe the restored graph).

9. Putting these together: the real "GA in the trenches"

These lessons converge on a plain, true methodology:

  1. Suspect initialization / registration / wiring before you suspect architecture. C4's Metadata, the pipeline's Replace, the coordinator's fallthrough, the DAGPatchExecutor fallback — all wiring details, none an algorithmic error.
  2. Delete cautiously, annotate why you keep. SchedulerGenomeName survives for historical data; the comment says why.
  3. For a dimension to be evolvable, you need an operator that produces a purely-different child. mutateSetMetadata only works because mutateReplaceNode preserves Metadata.
  4. Interfaces and configs must live off real evidence. Count callers for interface methods, verify config branches with tests, and measure performance with go test -bench (see 24.3).

10. Honest boundaries (important)

  • The previous 24.6's whole run-data story (three Scenarios, Best scores, lineage-improvement rates, prompt-mutation ratios, LLM final-check 85.9→70) and examples/autonomous-evolution/run.log → do not exist in the repo, are not reproducible, and this version no longer cites them.
  • If you need real evolution trajectories: run go run ./examples/10-ga-full-evolution (genuinely present in the repo), or use the 24.3 go test -bench for selection operators; when you cite, state the machine and flags.
  • This version only references facts verifiable in source comments / commits.

Appendix

[A] No invented performance or run data in this version. [B] Evidence you can read yourself: internal/runtime/evolution/genome/genome.go (interface slimming), internal/runtime/evolution/genome/workflow_genome.go (SchedulerGenomeName, C4, mutateSetMetadata), internal/runtime/evolution/candidate_pipeline.go (#25), internal/runtime/evolution/coordinator/coordinator.go (DefaultPolicy + fallthrough), internal/fabric/task/workflow/engine/dag_patcher.go (DAGPatchExecutor fallback).
